newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank Canada's Thiessen says less stimulus needed.
newsitem.headline: Bank Canada's Thiessen says less stimulus needed.

text.p: Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen said on Wednesday that as Canada absorbs its excess capacity, less monetary stimulus will be needed to keep the economy on the path of non-inflationary growth.

"Because we still have a fairly wide margin of spare production capacity in this country, our economy has ample room for strong growth in coming quarters without a resurgence of inflation," Thiessen said in a prepared speech to a business group. He added that "as that excess capacity is absorbed, less monetary stimulus will be needed to keep the Canadian economy on a non-inflationary growth path."
Thiessen said recent substantial interest rate cuts would continue to support robust growth in domestic spending.
"Because of the lags involved, the substantial past easing of interest rates should continue to support robust growth in domestic spending for some time," Thiessen said.
He said that monthly date for 1997 confirmed that there had been substantial increases in spending on housing, motor vehicles and consumer durables.
Thiessen said businesses were also increasing their capital spending.
"After a slow start to the year, growth in private sector employment has resumed, offsetting cutbacks and layoffs in the public sector," Thiessen said.

He said he believed the Canadian economy had reached the stage where the benefits from necessary adjustments had begun to outweigh the difficulties. He added that the Canadian economy was showing signs of responding to substantial declines in interest rates.
"It is only quite recently that signs of the response to those lower interest rates have become apparent," Thiessen said.
Thiessen said Canada's persistent current account deficit had been reduced because of the economy's export success and the reduced borrowing needs of Canadian governments.
"This means that as a nation we are no longer rapidly building up our indebtedness to foreigners," he said.

Thiessen said deficits had been reduced and governments had been moving toward less vulnerable debt positions. The ratio of government debt outstanding relative to the size of Canada's economy had started to decline and should continue to do so, he said.
"A decline in this ratio is essential to restore fully our financial health," Thiessen said.
He said that monetary policy was an important stabilizer for the economy, helping to maintain sustainable growth over time in output and employment.
Thiessen said the central bank expected solid economic growth and job gains through the rest of 1997.
"With our exports continuing to benefit from strong U.S. demand, the bank is looking for solid economic expansion and further employment gains through the year," he said.
The Bank remained committed to its inflation control targets," said Thiessen.

"While the targets were introduced to help reduce a high inflation rate, they continue to be the best means to conduct monetary policy now that inflation is low, and the aim is to keep it low," Thiessen said.
